set.overview: A non-technical walk to the high point of the Tahoe basin, following dirt road, then the Tahoe Rim Trail, then a steep spur up the ridge to the summit near 10,900 feet. The effort is in the sustained climbing and the altitude rather than any scrambling, and the top gives wide views over the lake and the Nevada desert.
set.approach: Drive Highway 89 between Hope Valley and Meyers and turn onto the unsigned dirt road that climbs toward Armstrong Pass, going three to four miles to a wide parking area before the road ends near Horse Meadow. A rough stretch or two favors ground clearance. From the parking area, cross the small creek and follow the old road about a mile up to Armstrong Pass, then turn right onto the Tahoe Rim Trail toward Star Lake. Continue about three miles to the saddle between Trimmer Peak and Freel Peak, where a sign marks the spur that leaves the rim trail and climbs the last mile to the top.
set.descent_text: Retrace the ascent: down the sandy spur to the signed saddle, then south along the Tahoe Rim Trail to Armstrong Pass and down the old road to the parking area. From the summit saddle toward Jobs Sister a faint use trail also drops toward Horse Meadow, but it needs route-finding, so the way you came up is the simple choice.
hazards: Soft granite sand over the last several hundred feet makes the final climb slow and the descent slippery.
The summit is near 10,900 feet, and altitude slows anyone who has not acclimatized.
The off-trail descent toward Horse Meadow has a few steep spots and no marked path.

evidence.fact: 2,530 ft gain, 9.3 mi out-and-back via Armstrong Pass and Tahoe Rim Trail
9.3 mi round trip, halved to 4.65 mi one-way = 7.48 km

review.notes: Gain and distance are single-source (Gaia out-and-back). The other page's 7.3 mi / 2,474 ft figure is a loop, so it was not used as a second source. Leg lengths on the two pages differ a little (Outbound legs sum to about 5 mi one way). Season skipped: no page gave months.

set.overview: The standard walk to the summit of Mount Tallac at 9,735 feet, entirely on trail inside Desolation Wilderness. It passes through forest and above Fallen Leaf Lake, goes by Floating Island Lake and Cathedral Lake, then crosses fully exposed boulders and a talus bowl to the ridge and a summit with all-round views.
set.approach: Drive Highway 89 about four miles north of the Y in South Lake Tahoe and turn west onto Mount Tallac Road, opposite the entrance to Baldwin Beach. Follow it about a mile, bearing left at a T-junction, to the trailhead at the road's end. A kiosk there issues the day-use wilderness pass. The road gate is locked from November through May, which adds about a mile of walking. The trail climbs through forest and along a ridge above Fallen Leaf Lake, then drops to Floating Island Lake and continues to Cathedral Lake, from which the summit is roughly 2.5 miles farther.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came, down the talus bowl and past Cathedral and Floating Island lakes to the trailhead. On the back side there is a signed junction where a tired party can miss the turn and head toward Gilmore Lake, so watch for it and keep to the trail you climbed.
hazards: Long stretches are fully exposed, so afternoon heat and summit wind and cold both matter.
Talus and scree on the upper trail give unstable footing.
Summer thunderstorms can arrive, and the trail has few markers above the lakes.
Snow can linger from late spring into early summer and may call for microspikes or an ice axe.
A signed junction on the descent can send a tired party toward Gilmore Lake.

review.notes: Season skipped: the page says generally summer and early fall with no months. Gain and distance were not in the fill list.

set.overview: An easy ridge-top walk on the Pacific Crest Trail to the summit of Tinker Knob, at about 8,950 feet. The trail runs at a gentle grade with one dip followed by a short climb, then switchbacks to a saddle, and a final quarter mile reaches the top. Views reach the American River canyon, Donner Lake and Lake Tahoe.
set.approach: Two ways reach the crest trail. From Olympic Valley, climb the Granite Chief Trail about 3.5 miles and 2,000 feet to the Pacific Crest Trail, then turn north along the crest about 3.5 miles toward the knob. A longer, easier approach comes along the crest trail from Donner Pass. Either way, the trail switchbacks up to the saddle just southeast of the peak, and a short final stretch of about a quarter mile leads to the summit.
set.descent_text: Walk back down the short summit spur to the saddle, then follow the Pacific Crest Trail the way you came, to Olympic Valley by the Granite Chief Trail or to Donner Pass, depending on where you started.

review.notes: One page. Hazards and season skipped: the page states none. Gain and distance were not in the fill list.
